q: Atoms and molecules are particles that make up matter.
e: This is a fundamental definition stated in the textbook.

q: In chemical calculations, chemists use relative masses of atoms and molecules on the basis of a designated standard unit mass, called atomic mass unit (amu).
e: The textbook explicitly defines amu as the designated standard unit mass for chemical calculations.

q: The mass of a single atom is so small that it is impossible to weigh it directly.
e: This is why relative atomic mass is used instead of direct weighing.

q: Scientists have chosen to use the isotope carbon-13 as the new standard because it is the most abundant isotope.
e: Scientists use carbon-12 as the standard because it is the most abundant isotope.

q: The relative atomic mass of an element is the average mass of one atom of the element compared with one twelfth the mass of one atom of the carbon-12 ($^{12} ext{C}$) isotope whose mass is exactly 12.
e: This is the exact definition of relative atomic mass provided in the text.

q: Atomic mass unit (amu) is precisely one twelfth the mass of one atom of carbon-12.
e: 1 amu equals one twelfth the mass of one atom of C-12 exactly.

q: To calculate the relative atomic mass of an element, we must know the isotopic masses of the various isotopes present and the relative abundance of the isotopes in nature.
e: Both isotopic masses and their relative abundances are required for this calculation.

q: The relative molecular mass ($M_r$) of a molecule is the mass of one molecule of a substance on a scale where the carbon-12 isotopes has a mass of exactly 12 units (12 amu).
e: This is the exact definition of relative molecular mass.

q: For ionic compounds, we use the term relative molecular mass instead of relative formula mass.
e: For ionic compounds, we use the term relative formula mass instead of relative molecular mass.

q: The relative formula mass of an ionic compound is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula.
e: This is the correct definition of relative formula mass for ionic compounds.

q: A magnesium atom has twice the mass of a $^{12} ext{C}$ atom, so its relative atomic mass is 24.
e: Based on the example, 2 x 12 = 24, which is the relative atomic mass of magnesium.

q: The average relative atomic mass of magnesium is calculated using only the isotopic masses, ignoring their relative abundances in nature.
e: The calculation requires both the isotopic masses and their relative abundances in nature.

q: A symbol is a shorthand notation of an element.
e: This is the exact definition of a chemical symbol.

q: The first letter in the name of an element is usually chosen as the symbol of the element.
e: This is the standard rule for assigning chemical symbols.

q: When the names of two or more elements begin with the same letter, the first letter together with another letter in the name of an element is chosen as the symbol.
e: This rule prevents ambiguity in chemical symbols.

q: A symbol represents a molecule of the element and the mass of an atom.
e: A symbol represents an atom of the element and the mass of an atom, not a molecule.

q: The symbols of some elements are taken from English names, while others are taken from Latin names.
e: The textbook provides tables showing both English and Latin derived symbols.

q: The symbol for Sodium is Na, taken from its Latin name Natrium.
e: Sodium's symbol Na is derived from its Latin name Natrium.

q: The symbol for Potassium is P, taken from its Latin name Kalium.
e: The symbol for Potassium is K, taken from its Latin name Kalium.

q: The symbol for Iron is Fe, taken from its Latin name Ferrum.
e: Iron's symbol Fe is derived from its Latin name Ferrum.

q: A molecular formula is a shorthand notation representing a molecule or a compound of a substance.
e: This is the exact definition of a molecular formula.

q: A molecular formula shows the number of atoms contained in a molecule or a compound.
e: This is a key function of a molecular formula.

q: For example, $2 ext{O}_2$ means two molecules of oxygen.
e: The coefficient 2 indicates two separate molecules of $	ext{O}_2$.

q: For those compounds which exist in the form of giant structure, a formula represents the simplest unit of the compound.
e: Giant structures do not have separate molecules, so the formula represents the simplest unit.

q: As compounds of giant structure do not have separate molecules, they cannot have molecular mass, so formula mass is used instead.
e: This explains why formula mass is the correct term for giant structures.

q: The empirical formula of a compound is the simplest formula of the compound.
e: This is the exact definition of an empirical formula.

q: The empirical formula shows the types of elements present in the compound and the simplest ratio of the different types of the atoms in the compound.
e: These are the two specific pieces of information shown by an empirical formula.

q: An empirical formula can also be deduced from data that give the percentage composition by mass of the elements in a compound.
e: Percentage composition by mass is a valid starting point for deducing an empirical formula.

q: When the empirical and molecular formulae of a compound are different, the molecular formula is always a multiple of the empirical formula.
e: The molecular formula is always a whole number multiple of the empirical formula.

q: Molecular formula = $n imes$ empirical formula, where $n$ is 1, 2, 3, 4...
e: This is the exact mathematical relationship between molecular and empirical formulae.

q: The empirical formula of phosphorus(V) oxide is $ ext{P}_2 ext{O}_5$, while its actual molecular formula is $ ext{P}_4 ext{O}_{10}$.
e: This is the specific example given in the textbook to illustrate the difference.

q: The formula of a compound and relative atomic masses can be used to calculate the percentage by mass of a particular element in a compound.
e: This is the stated purpose of percentage composition by mass calculations.

q: The combining capacity or valence of an element is represented by the number of atoms of hydrogen, chlorine or sodium that combine with one atom of that element.
e: This is the exact definition of combining capacity or valence.

q: The element sodium reacts with other elements to form compounds in which it shows electropositive character and a constant combining capacity of 1.
e: Sodium consistently exhibits a combining capacity of 1.

q: Oxidation number describes the combining capacity of the element and also indicates the positive and negative nature of its atoms in the compounds.
e: This is the exact definition of oxidation number provided in the text.

q: The oxidation number is identical with valence or combining capacity.
e: The oxidation number is related to, but not identical with, valence or combining capacity.

q: In compounds formed by the combination of metals with non-metals, metals always show electropositive character.
e: Metals consistently show electropositive character in such compounds.

q: In compounds formed by the combination of one non-metal with another, the more electropositive element is assigned a positive oxidation number and the other is assigned a negative oxidation number.
e: This is the rule for assigning oxidation numbers in non-metal compounds.

q: A binary compound is a compound which contains two elements only.
e: This is the exact definition of a binary compound.

q: In the formula of a binary compound, the more electropositive element present in the compound with positive oxidation number is written in front of the symbol of the element with negative oxidation number.
e: This is the standard rule for ordering symbols in a binary compound formula.

q: $ ext{NH}_3$ is an exception in which the symbol with negative oxidation number (N) is written first.
e: Ammonia is explicitly noted as an exception to the standard ordering rule.

q: In the formula of a compound, the algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers must be equal to zero.
e: This is the fundamental rule for writing correct chemical formulae.

q: Binary compounds in which the more electropositive element with fixed oxidation number is in the first place are named with the name of the second element ending in -ide.
e: This is the standard naming convention for such binary compounds.

q: For the naming of non-metallic binary compounds with variable oxidation numbers, Greek prefixes (e.g., mono-, di-, tri-, etc.) are used to indicate the number of atoms of each element.
e: Greek prefixes are specifically used for non-metallic binary compounds with variable oxidation numbers.

q: For naming metallic binary compounds with variable oxidation numbers, the name of the more electropositive metallic element is given first, followed by the Roman Numeral in brackets to state its oxidation number, and the name of the second element ending in -ide.
e: This is the exact naming rule for metallic binary compounds with variable oxidation numbers.

q: The formula of hydrochloric acid is $ ext{HCl}$. When H is removed from the formula, the remaining part is $ ext{Cl}^-$, which represents the acid radical of hydrochloric acid.
e: This correctly describes the formation of the chloride acid radical.

q: In naming acids which have hydrogen atoms in their molecules, the name of the acid radical -ic is changed to -ide.
e: For example, hydrochloric acid yields the chloride radical.

q: In naming acids which have oxygen atoms in their molecules, the -ous acid radical is changed to -ate.
e: The -ous acid radical is changed to -ite, while the -ic acid radical is changed to -ate.

q: In naming the acid radicals containing H, the word hydrogen is placed before the name of the acid radical.
e: For example, $	ext{HSO}_4^-$ is named hydrogen sulphate.

q: The ion formed after removal of hydroxide ions ($ ext{OH}^-$ ions) from a base is called a basic radical.
e: This is the exact definition of a basic radical.

q: The formula of a salt consists of two parts: the first part is the metal atom or the ammonium radical, and the second part is the acid radical.
e: This describes the standard composition of a salt formula.

q: When writing the formula of a salt, the algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers must be equal to one.
e: The algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers must be equal to zero.

q: Hydroxides are named in the same way as the naming of salts, but the name of the acid radical is replaced by the word hydroxide.
e: This is the specific rule for naming hydroxides.

q: The Roman Numeral represents the oxidation number of the metal atom in a salt with a variable oxidation number.
e: The textbook explicitly states that the Roman Numeral indicates the metal's oxidation number.

q: All hydroxides include one or more $- ext{OH}$ radicals of oxidation number -1 in their formulae.
e: This is a defining characteristic of all hydroxide compounds.

q: The formula of sulphuric acid is $ ext{H}_2 ext{SO}_4$, and when one H is removed, the remaining part $- ext{HSO}_4$ represents one acid radical of sulphuric acid.
e: This correctly describes the stepwise formation of acid radicals from sulphuric acid.

q: The acid radical of nitric acid ($ ext{HNO}_3$) is nitrate ($ ext{NO}_3^-$).
e: This matches the data provided in Table 4.5 of the textbook.

q: The relative atomic masses of elements as well as the relative molecular masses of ions or compounds expressed in amu are not feasible to be used in the weighable scale, especially in grams.
e: The text states that amu is not feasible for weighable scales, necessitating the mole concept.

q: The chemists' counting unit is named the mole, and it is defined as equal to the number of atoms in exactly 12 g of $^{12} ext{C}$.
e: This is the exact definition of the mole.

q: This number of particles is called Avogadro's constant, which is equal to $6.02 imes 10^{23}$.
e: This is the accepted value of Avogadro's constant stated in the text.

q: We may refer to the mass of a mole of substance as its molar mass (abbreviation M).
e: Molar mass is the correct term for the mass of one mole of a substance.

q: The unit of molar mass is $ ext{g mol}^{-1}$.
e: This is the standard SI-derived unit for molar mass.

q: One mole of a substance is the amount of substance that has the same number of particles (atoms, molecules, etc.) as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of $^{12} ext{C}$.
e: This is the formal definition of one mole.

q: The Avogadro's constant applies only to atoms and molecules, not to ions and electrons.
e: The Avogadro's constant applies to atoms, molecules, ions, and electrons.

q: A mole of chlorine molecules, $ ext{Cl}_2$, contains $6.02 imes 10^{23}$ chlorine molecules but twice as many chlorine atoms.
e: Since each $	ext{Cl}_2$ molecule has two atoms, there are twice as many atoms as molecules.

q: Amedeo Avogadro first deduced that equal volumes of gases contain equal number of molecules under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.
e: This is the historical fact attributed to Amedeo Avogadro in the text.

q: One mole of any gas has a volume of $24 ext{ dm}^3$ or $24,000 ext{ cm}^3$ at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.).
e: This is the defined molar volume of a gas at r.t.p.

q: Room temperature and pressure are often taken as conditions of $25^{\circ} ext{C}$ and 1 atmosphere.
e: These are the specific conditions defined as r.t.p. in the textbook.

q: One mole of every gas occupies $22.4 ext{ dm}^3$ at STP (standard temperature, $0^{\circ} ext{C}$ or 273 K and standard pressure, 760 mmHg or 1 atmosphere).
e: This is the defined molar volume of a gas at STP.

q: The Systeme International (SI) unit for mass is the gram.
e: The SI unit for mass is the kilogram, though chemists often use grams for convenience.

q: Chemists prefer to use the relative molecular mass or formula mass in grams.
e: Grams are preferred over kilograms for general laboratory work in chemistry.

q: Number of moles (mol) = mass of a substance in gram (g) / molar mass ($ ext{g mol}^{-1}$).
e: This is the correct formula for calculating the number of moles from mass.

q: Mass of substance (g) = number of moles (mol) $ imes$ molar mass ($ ext{g mol}^{-1}$).
e: This is the correct rearranged formula for calculating mass from moles.

q: Equal volumes of gases contain equal number of molecules at the same temperature and pressure.
e: This is Avogadro's law, as stated in the key terms.

q: The Avogadro's constant is the number of entities or a stated type of particles in a mole of those substances.
e: This is the exact definition of Avogadro's constant from the key terms.

q: In 1 mole of sodium chloride ($ ext{NaCl}$) there are $6.02 imes 10^{23}$ sodium ions and $6.02 imes 10^{23}$ chloride ions.
e: The text explicitly states this breakdown for ionic compounds like NaCl.

q: The molar volume of a gas is the volume occupied by one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure.
e: This is the definition of molar volume provided in the text.
